newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Conrail head disputes Norfolk offer.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Conrail head disputes Norfolk offer.

text.p: The former chairman of Conrail Inc, testifying in a federal court hearing on Tuesday, denied that Norfolk Southern Corp had offered in 1994 to acquire Conrail for 1.1 shares of Norfolk Southern.
Asked in court whether it was true he had declined such an offer from Norfolk Southern Chairman David Goode, former Conrail chairman James Hagen said that was "not correct."

"I suggested that I would recommend to the board of directors (an offer) at 1.1 (to one)," Hagen said. It was Goode who declined those terms after earlier suggesting a 1.05 to one swap would be acceptable, he told the court.

Norfolk Southern has argued in court papers that it had offered Conrail the deal in 1994, and therefore Conrail directors should have known when pursuing a merger with CSX Corp that a strong offer from another bidder was available.

Norfolk Southern has said an exchange at that rate would have been worth $101 per Conrail share in October 1996, when Conrail announced a merger agreement with CSX worth an estimated $92.50 per share. CSX has since raised its offer.

Norfolk Southern has sued in federal court to block the first step of the Conrail-CSX merger, a tender offer by CSX for 19.9 percent of Conrail's shares. Norfolk Southern says Conrail improperly entered into a merger agreement with CSX that precludes the possibilities of higher offers.
Hagen was testifying on the second day of hearings into the case.
Judge Donald Van Artsdalen indicated on Monday he hoped to conclude the hearing by 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time, Tuesday, but on Tuesday morning testimony was running more than an hour behind schedule.
Both Conrail and Norfolk Southern indicated Tuesday they would immediately appeal any adverse ruling.

Separately from the testimony, a Norfolk Southern brief on the case, orginally filed under seal, argued that a Delaware court's decision in the 1993-1994 takeover battle for Paramount Inc could serve as a precedent for this case.

In that case, Norfolk Southern said, the Delaware Supreme Court ruled that the board of Paramount violated its fiduciary duties once a rival bidder, QVC Inc, emerged for Paramount. That court said Paramount improperly tightened "lockup" provisions in its orginal deal with Viacom Inc, and the court ordered an auction for the company be conducted.
Similarly, Norfolk Southern argued in its brief, Conrail's board improperly tightened its lockups with CSX after Norfolk Southern emerged with a higher bid.

"Given the similar facts, a similar result is called for in this case," Norfolk Southern said. "There is no justification ... for reincorporating them (the lock-ups), with added muscle, in the amended transaction adopted following Norfolk Southern's initial offer."
A current Conrail board member, H. Furlong Baldwin, said in court yesterday that the strong lock-up provisions were needed to ensure that CSX did not walk away from the deal.

Conrail, a Pennsylvania corporation, is not governed by Delaware law, but rulings in that state can have influence because of the many major corporations incorporated there and the large body of case law that has evolved.
